decisions.why: 118.9 itself defines an alternative cost as a cost the controller may pay rather than the spell's mana cost, which is exactly what Archive Trap's free cast is.
810.9's own text says damage, loss of life, and gaining life happen to each player individually, and none of 810.9a-h speaks to targeting teammates separately.
101.2 itself states that a 'can't' effect takes precedence over an effect that allows something; 101.2a is only an unrelated carve-out for adding and removing abilities.
105.2 only frames how many colors an object can be; 105.2c is the sentence that says a colorless object has no color.
106.4 itself says mana can stay in the pool as unspent mana and empties at end of step or phase, so nothing forces Atlas to spend it.
106.6 itself says mana-producing effects can restrict how that mana is spent; 106.6a only covers replacement effects that increase the amount produced.
603.3 itself says a triggered ability goes on the stack the next time a player would receive priority, i.e. after Essence Feed has finished resolving.
101.2 itself states the 'can't' effect wins, which is why Arcane Denial cannot counter an uncounterable spell; 101.2a is unrelated.
113.10 itself states that effects can remove abilities from objects; none of 113.10a-c addresses an ability being stripped in the graveyard.
101.2 itself states that a 'can't' effect takes precedence over an effect that would allow prevention.
615.12's own text says prevention effects applied to unpreventable damage won't prevent any of it; 615.12a only stops a prevention effect from re-invoking itself.
202.3 itself defines mana value as the total amount of mana in an object's mana cost, which is the general rule the judge's answer starts from.
603.2 itself says an ability triggers whenever a game event matches its trigger event, which is why Mindcrank triggers mid-resolution.
603.3 itself says the triggered ability is put on the stack the next time a player would receive priority, i.e. after Vampiric Tutor finishes resolving.
101.2 itself states the 'can't' effect takes precedence, which caps the counters Clockwork Beast can receive.
903.3 only says each deck designates a commander; 903.3d is the sentence saying an effect that refers to controlling a commander means any permanent that is a commander.
115.1 itself says targets are declared as part of putting the spell on the stack, so a spell that declares none has no targets; no 115.1 child covers a creature spell with a copy replacement effect.
115.10 itself states that spells and abilities can affect objects they don't target.
616.1 itself states that when two or more replacement effects would modify an event, the affected object's controller chooses which to apply.
103.5 itself says that once a player chooses not to take a mulligan that player may not take any further mulligans.
608.2 is a step-ordering header; 608.2n is the sentence stating the spell is put into its owner's graveyard as the final part of resolution.
709.4 supplies the necessary 'in every zone except the stack' framing and 709.4b is the sentence deriving a split card's colors from its combined mana cost.
715.2 itself states the inset frame defines alternative characteristics the object may have while it's a spell, the premise for Kellan having two castable sides.
715.3 itself says the player chooses whether to play the card normally or as an Adventure, which is the answer.
715.2's own text limits the Adventure's alternative characteristics to while the object is a spell, so in the graveyard the card has only its creature characteristics.
506.4's list of removal-from-combat events never mentions untapping; 506.4b is the sentence saying untapping a declared attacker doesn't remove it from combat.
602.2 itself states that activating an ability is putting it on the stack and then paying its costs, in the steps listed in order, which is the sequencing the answer rests on.
715.2's own text limits the Adventure's alternative characteristics to while the object is a spell, so in the graveyard Blessed Hippogriff is only a creature card.
610.4 only describes the 'phases out until' mechanic; 610.4a is the sentence saying such a permanent doesn't phase in from the untap step's turn-based action.
707.9 is a bare header for copy-effect exceptions; 707.9b states that a characteristic modified during copying becomes part of the copy's copiable values.
709.4 gives the necessary 'every zone except the stack' rule and 709.4c is the sentence saying a split card has each card type of both halves.
709.3 itself says the player chooses which half they are casting before putting it on the stack, so either half is legal.
109.2 itself says a card-type or subtype description with no zone and no 'card'/'spell'/'source' means a permanent of that subtype on the battlefield, so the Elk no longer qualifies as a Food.
603.10 only says some triggers look back in time; 603.10a is the sentence putting leaves-the-battlefield abilities on that list.
101.4 itself defines APNAP order for simultaneous choices, which sets the order the two triggers are put on the stack.
707.10 itself states that a copy of a spell isn't cast, which is why the replicate copies don't trigger Chalice of the Void.
607.1 itself says a linked ability refers only to objects affected by its partner ability and not by any other ability, so each Augury sees only the cards it exiled.
118.12 states the '[do something]' action is a cost paid on resolution, and 118.12a is what maps Curse Artifact's 'unless' wording onto that template.
106.4 itself says each player's mana pool empties at the end of each step and phase, which is why the mana is gone by the declare attackers step.
614.12 itself says the game checks the permanent's characteristics as it would exist on the battlefield to work out how it enters; 614.12a covers only effects requiring a choice, which this isn't.
603.1 itself defines the trigger-condition-and-effect form of a triggered ability, and neither 603.1a nor 603.1b bears on a dies trigger.
603.10 only says some triggers look back in time; 603.10a is the sentence that puts leaves-the-battlefield abilities on that list.
613.1 supplies the necessary rule that continuous effects are applied in layer order, and 613.1e/f/g are the specific layers this answer walks through.
613.4 gives the general rule that layer 7 is resolved in sublayers, and 613.4b/c are the setting and modifying sublayers the answer uses.
613.7 states the timestamp-order rule the answer turns on and 613.7a supplies the timestamp of an effect generated by a static ability.
707.2 itself defines what a copy acquires, the copiable values of the object being copied, which is the rule Sakashima's illegal enchantment copy is measured against.
616.1 itself says the affected player chooses which of the competing replacement effects to apply.
614.7 itself says a replacement effect whose event never happens simply does nothing, which is why the second draw replacement drops out; 614.7a is only the 0-damage case.
400.7 itself says an object that changes zones becomes a new object with no memory of its previous existence; every 400.7 child is an exception that doesn't apply here.
903.3 itself says the commander designation is an attribute of the card that it retains even when it changes zones, so the face-down card is still a commander.
616.1 itself states the affected object's controller chooses which replacement effect to apply, one at a time.
616.1 itself states the affected object's controller chooses the order the competing replacement effects are applied in.
707.2 itself defines copiable values, which is what each of the two copy effects overwrites.
613.7 states that effects in a layer are applied in timestamp order and 613.7b supplies the timestamp for an effect created by a resolving spell or ability.
707.2 itself lists mana cost among the copiable values a copy acquires, which is why the token copy of Jibbirik Omnivore isn't mana value 0.
614.12 itself says to check the characteristics of the permanent as it would exist on the battlefield, so Minas Tirith is seen as a creature.
613.7 states the timestamp-order rule and 613.7a gives the timestamp of a continuous effect generated by a static ability, which is what orders Conversion before Magus of the Moon.
614.12 itself says to check the permanent's characteristics as it would exist on the battlefield, so Erebos is not seen as a creature.
616.1 only says the affected player chooses; 616.1a is the sentence that forces a self-replacement effect like Memory Lapse's to be applied first.
704.5 is a bare list header ('The state-based actions are as follows'); 704.5g is the lethal-damage state-based action that regeneration can replace.

106.6 only says mana-producing effects can create restrictions or delayed triggers; 106.6a is the sentence saying a separate delayed trigger is created for each mana when a replacement effect increases the amount.
727.1 itself says a restarted game ends immediately and all players then start a new game under rule 103, which is what creates the new first turn.
202.1 itself defines a card's mana cost as the mana symbols printed on the card, so what was actually paid doesn't change it.
406.3 itself states that cards exiled face down can't be examined by any player except when instructions allow it, which frames what Nixon can know.
708.2 itself says face-down permanents have no characteristics other than those listed by the ability that turned them face down, so Skullbriar loses its counter-keeping ability.
118.12 itself says the '[do something]' action in that template is a cost paid on resolution, the rule the judge cites by number.
113.6 itself says abilities of objects other than instants and sorceries function only while on the battlefield, so Compost does nothing from the graveyard.
603.10's normal rule (objects are checked immediately after the event) is what applies to Compost, and 603.10a is the exception list Compost's 'from anywhere' trigger fails to fit.
118.12a is the sentence rewriting 'draw a card unless that player pays {1}' as 'that player may pay; if they don't, draw', which is what makes Alex choose first.
614.12 gives the rule that entry replacement effects are worked out from the permanent as it would exist on the battlefield, and 614.12a states the choice is made before it enters.
616.1 itself states the affected object's controller chooses which competing replacement effect to apply.
113.6 itself says abilities of a permanent function only while it's on the battlefield, so All-Seeing Arbiter can't trigger once it's been sacrificed.
106.12 itself defines 'tap for mana' as activating a mana ability that includes {T} in its cost, which Deathrite Shaman's ability is not.
727.1 itself says all players start a new game following the rule 103 procedures, which is when a companion would be announced again.
613.7 supplies the timestamp-order rule the answer turns on, and 613.7a/b/d give the specific timestamps for the static ability, the resolved spell, and the object entering a zone.
729.2 itself says to randomly determine which player goes first in the subgame.
727.1 itself says all players in the game when it ended then start a new game, which is why the restarted game is a two-player game.
613.7 states the timestamp-order rule and 613.7b gives the timestamp of the continuous effect created by Turn to Frog resolving.
616.1 itself states the affected object's controller chooses which replacement effect to apply, and the process it heads is what puts the control-change first.
508.1 itself says the active player follows the declare-attackers steps in order, which is why the restriction check happens before creatures become attacking creatures.
614.12 gives the rule that entry replacement effects are determined before the permanent enters, and 614.12a states the required choice is made before it enters.
614.10 states that a skip is a replacement effect that waits for the next occurrence, and 614.10b is the sentence putting the follow-up action at the start of the next turn that actually happens.
